title: DRC announces new four-month cobalt export ban
gist: The DRC's ARECOMS will ban all cobalt exports for four months from 30 November 2026, capping 2027 DRC exports at 65,250t (removing 29kt). Benchmark says this widens the 2027 deficit from -22kt to -40kt, or to -127kt when only exportable material is counted. Analyst Roman Aubry expects a significant price impact. The market had expected tighter quotas rather than a full ban, after hydroxide fell from $23.75/lb in July to $12.50/lb in mid-November.

insights.claim: ARECOMS, the DRC's governing body for strategic minerals, will ban all cobalt exports for four months starting 30 November 2026.
insights.speaker: Roman Aubry, George Ingall, Matthew Bird
insights.so_what: A renewed outright export halt from the largest cobalt source is a direct supply shock for cobalt prices and refiners.
insights.quote: will implement a four month ban on all cobalt exports from 30 November 2026
insights.locator: The DRC’s governing body for strategic minerals

insights.claim: The DRC previously banned cobalt exports in February 2025 and then let specific miners resume exports under a quota system in October 2025, before announcing a new four-month ban from 30 November 2026.
insights.speaker: Roman Aubry, George Ingall, Matthew Bird
insights.so_what: The DRC has shown it will toggle between bans and quotas, so cobalt supply policy is a recurring, not one-off, risk.
insights.locator: The DRC’s governing body for strategic minerals

insights.claim: Most market participants Benchmark spoke with expected ARECOMS to respond to falling cobalt prices by tightening export quotas, not by imposing an outright ban, so the November 2026 ban was more severe than the market anticipated.
insights.speaker: Roman Aubry, George Ingall, Matthew Bird
insights.so_what: Because the market was positioned for a milder quota cut, the full ban is more likely to move prices.
insights.quote: the majority of conversations between Benchmark and the market pointed towards the expectation that ARECOMS would tighten quotas rather than issuing an outright ban
insights.locator: How has the previous ban impacted

insights.claim: Market participants perceive the DRC's cobalt export restrictions as a tool to control cobalt prices, and expected the DRC to act when hydroxide prices fell rapidly in late 2026.
insights.speaker: Roman Aubry, George Ingall, Matthew Bird
insights.so_what: If the DRC effectively defends a price floor, cobalt downside is limited by policy risk.
insights.quote: particularly given the perception that the DRC had implemented export restrictions to better control cobalt prices
insights.locator: How has the previous ban impacted

themes.theme: Cobalt market balance after the ban

insights.claim: With the new ban, DRC cobalt exports for 2027 are capped at 65,250 tonnes, removing 29,000 tonnes of cobalt from the market.
insights.speaker: Roman Aubry, George Ingall, Matthew Bird
insights.so_what: A 29kt cut is a large share of the market and tightens 2027 supply.
insights.quote: DRC exports for 2027 are capped at 65,250 tonnes, removing 29,000 tonnes of cobalt available to the market

insights.claim: Benchmark estimates the new DRC cobalt export ban widens the cobalt market deficit from -48kt to -54kt in 2026 and from -22kt to -40kt in 2027.
insights.speaker: Roman Aubry, George Ingall, Matthew Bird
insights.so_what: The 2027 cobalt deficit nearly doubles under Benchmark's balance, which supports higher prices.
insights.quote: This pushes the deficit in 2026 from -48kt to -54kt, and from -22kt to -40kt in 2027

insights.claim: Benchmark's headline cobalt balance includes CMOC material that cannot be exported, so it overstates what downstream refiners can get; counting only material that can leave the DRC, the 2027 cobalt deficit grows to -127kt.
insights.speaker: Roman Aubry, George Ingall, Matthew Bird
insights.so_what: Supply available to refiners is much tighter than the headline deficit; look at export-constrained balances, not mined output.
insights.locator: This market balance includes unexportable CMOC

insights.claim: Benchmark cobalt analyst Roman Aubry expects the new DRC export ban to have a significant impact on cobalt prices, made worse by unconfirmed rumours of Indonesian HPAL cuts.
insights.speaker: Roman Aubry, George Ingall, Matthew Bird
insights.so_what: Two supply risks at once (DRC ban plus possible Indonesian HPAL cuts) raise the chance of a sharp cobalt price rally.
insights.quote: This is likely to have a significant impact on prices; compounded by the unconfirmed Indonesian rumours on HPAL cuts
insights.locator: This is likely to have a significant

insights.claim: During 2026, DRC miners could export cobalt but struggled to sell hydroxide because cheaper alternatives pushed buyers to seek lower offers, so hydroxide stocks built up in warehouses outside the DRC.
insights.speaker: Roman Aubry, George Ingall, Matthew Bird
insights.so_what: Cobalt hydroxide stocks sitting outside the DRC will cushion the ban at first and give holders a chance to sell at higher prices.
insights.quote: hydroxide stocks have grown in ex-DRC warehouses
insights.locator: This is likely to have a significant

insights.claim: Roman Aubry says the shift in sentiment after the DRC ban gives miners and traders a chance to sell already-exported cobalt held in warehouses around China at higher prices.
insights.speaker: Roman Aubry, George Ingall, Matthew Bird
insights.so_what: Holders of cobalt stock in China are the near-term winners from the ban; destocking may cap the first price spike.
insights.quote: there is an opportunity for miners and traders to leverage this to sell already exported material sitting in warehouses around China at higher price levels

insights.claim: After the DRC's February 2025 cobalt export ban, cobalt hydroxide prices more than doubled in three months, from $5.70/lb to $11.75/lb.
insights.speaker: Roman Aubry, George Ingall, Matthew Bird
insights.so_what: Sets a benchmark for how fast cobalt prices can react to a DRC export halt.
insights.quote: Cobalt hydroxide prices more than doubled in the three months following the ban, from $5.70/lb to $11.75/lb
insights.locator: How has the previous ban impacted

insights.claim: High cobalt prices after the 2025 DRC ban led downstream refiners to switch to recycled sulphate from black mass and MHP from Indonesia, feedstocks that had usually been less competitive.
insights.speaker: Roman Aubry, George Ingall, Matthew Bird
insights.so_what: High prices pull in substitute supply from recycling and Indonesian nickel-cobalt intermediates, which limits how long a DRC-driven rally lasts.
insights.quote: Recycled sulphate from black mass and MHP from Indonesia bridged the gap for the limited hydroxide

insights.claim: Bearish sentiment among downstream Chinese refiners limited buying of cobalt hydroxide in 2026 even though the market was fundamentally tight.
insights.speaker: Roman Aubry, George Ingall, Matthew Bird
insights.so_what: Chinese refiner sentiment can override tight fundamentals, so it is the swing factor for cobalt prices.
insights.quote: despite fundamental tightness in the market

insights.claim: Cobalt hydroxide prices started falling in August 2026, from $23.75/lb at the end of July to $12.50/lb in mid-November.
insights.speaker: Roman Aubry, George Ingall, Matthew Bird
insights.so_what: A roughly 47% drop from the peak sets up the new ban as a catalyst for a rebound from depressed levels.
